old: In this guide, subconscious means the deeper processes shaping perception, emotion, desire, avoidance, imagery, memory, bodily signals, habits, intuition, and automatic behavior. Sometimes it helps to address all of that as one mind; sometimes an ecology of parts gives more precision. Both are maps. Neither needs its own priesthood.
Parts give precision. Higher Self gives coherence. Communion is the movement between them.
When you need coherence, speak to the deeper mind as a whole:
“Wise subconscious, please help me understand.”

When you need precision, notice the different tendencies inside it: the child wanting love, the protector wanting safety, the critic wanting standards, the fantasy-maker wanting possibility, the body memory wanting recognition, the social self wanting belonging, the spiritual self wanting God or source or the benefit of all beings, and the wiser part wanting what is true.
Begin with unity when the system feels scattered:
“Higher Self, universal heart-mind, wise subconscious, please guide me.”
Differentiate only when the question needs it:
“Which part of me is afraid?” “Which part is protecting?” “Which part is avoiding?” “Which part knows the next step?” “Which part is too young to carry this?”
Then bring the parts back into one life:
“Let all of this belong to one life. Let the adult self lead with love.”
new: In my guides when I refer to your ‘subconscious’ I am referring to everything going on beneath the surface of your conscious mind – perceptions, emotions, desires, aversions, imagery, memories, body signals, habits, intuitions, automatic behaviours etc. Sometimes it is useful to work with all of these as one ‘mind’, other times it can be more effective to work with the ‘ecology’ of parts. Neither way is ‘right’ or ‘wrong’ it is just a question of using the right map for the job in hand.
Working with parts is about precision, working with the Higher Self is about coherence – you need to move in and out of communion with both.
To work with the ‘whole’ – the subconscious as one:
“Invoke” the subconscious – e.g. ‘Hello wise subconscious can you help me understand…..’

To work with ‘parts’ recognise the ‘ecology’ in the subconscious – there may be a child part that wants love, a protector part that wants to keep you safe, a ‘critic’ that wants you to live up to certain standards, a fantasy making part, body memory parts, a social part, a spiritual part that wants to connect to God/source/do what is in the best benefit of all beings, a ‘wiser’ part etc etc
Generally it is a good idea to start with unity:
“Invoke” your Higher Self – e.g. ‘Hello my Higher Self/universal heart-mind/wise subconscious please can you help me…..’
Then move into differentiation if needed:
Ask “Which part is afraid? Which part is protecting? Which part is avoiding? Which part knows what to do? Which part is too young for this?”
Then move back into unity – recognising that it is all part of the same life and ideally all parts should be led by the ‘adult’ self operating from a place of love.

old: Some people feel more fragmented when they begin by naming twelve parts and assigning everybody office space. Start with the sacred whole when that happens.
new: For some people, it is better not to start by asking for the 12 parts, or by giving everybody an office. For these people, it is better to start from the Sacred whole.

old: “I begin from the universal heart. I begin from Higher Self. I begin from the part of me that belongs to life before it belongs to any wound, role, family, group, identity, ideology, or story. Please help me understand what is true, kind, timely, stabilizing, and useful.”
new: In order to do this, I start with a prayer: ‘Let’s begin by connecting to the universal heart (or to my Higher Self). The universal heart (or the Higher Self) is the part of me that existed before I was born and that will exist after I am gone. It is the part of me that is not wounded, the part of me that is not caught in any roles, or families or groups. The part of me that has no identities, no ideologies, and no stories. From this place, let’s ask for what is true, kind, timely, stabilizing and useful.’

old: If Higher Self, the universal heart, or any sacred language feels unavailable or borrowed from somebody else, begin with plain witnessing instead. Notice the room, the body, and the younger state. The fact that something can notice is enough adult presence for the first step.
new: Sometimes, people don’t have access to their Higher Self, or to the universal heart, or whatever language you might use that feels sacred for you. In that case, I’ll just begin by asking them to start witnessing, to notice things around them, or in their body, or to notice that they are in a younger state. The fact that they can notice is usually enough of an adult function to begin with.

old: If you can already notice and distinguish what is happening inside, you don’t need to keep rehearsing the Witness. Work with the warmth, protection, or direction that is actually missing. Higher Self language can help you gather around a meaningful source of care; it doesn’t establish that a perfectly capable inner parent is already available. Those adult functions still grow through practice.
new: Once people can notice, and distinguish, there’s no point in working more on their Witness. Begin working on whatever else they need: warmth, protection, direction etc. So while the language of the Higher Self is useful in order to bring people together, it doesn’t mean that all the adult functions are already there. You’ll need to work on growing them.

old: Differentiate only when something specific appears:
“Is this the inner child?” “Is this a protector?” “Is this the body?” “Is this fear?” “Is this intuition?” “Is this social conditioning?” “Is this divine guidance, or my interpretation of guidance?”
Start from the heart. Differentiate only as needed. Return to the heart.
new: It is important to differentiate but only as needed when something comes up. “Is this coming from my inner child? Is it a protector? Is this my body speaking? Is this fear speaking? Is this intuition? Is this social conditioning speaking? Is this divine guidance or my interpretation of guidance?”
But always start from the heart, differentiate as needed, and then come back to the heart.

old: Use this checklist when a person, advertisement, ideology, spiritual teaching, romantic pull, or inner voice is pressing too hard.

“I notice influence is happening. I do not need to obey it or attack it. I can slow down. I can ask what is being presupposed. I can ask who benefits. I can notice what my body is signaling without assuming what it proves. I can ask what love, truth, humility, and ordinary life would require.

If this is true, it will survive questions. If this is love, it will survive boundaries. If this is guidance, it will survive sleep. If this is for me, it will not require me to abandon my adult self.”
Before acting, ask:
Is there urgency?
Is there secrecy?
Is there shame?
Is there a threat of exclusion?
Is there a promise of specialness?
Is there sexual charge?
Is there spiritual superiority?
Is there a demand for money, sex, loyalty, silence, or obedience?
Is there a narrowing of choices?
Is questioning treated as betrayal?
Is resistance pathologized?
Is ordinary life being downgraded?
new: Things to Consider When Influence is Occurring
Take a Time Out and say to yourself:

I see that influence is occurring. I don’t have to act on it. I don’t have to attack it. I can take a time out. I can consider what is being presupposed here. I can consider who benefits here. I can pay attention to what my body is telling me, without believing it tells the whole story. I can ask some questions, such as how does this square with love? How does this square with truth? How does this square with humility? How does this fit with ordinary life?

Then say to yourself: If it’s true, it will survive the passage of time. If it’s love, it will survive the passage of time. If it’s what I’m supposed to do, it will survive the passage of time. If it’s really for me, it will survive my being an adult.
Then ask yourself: Is there any …

sense of urgency? sense of secrecy? sense of shame? threatening to not include me if I don’t do what I’m being influenced to do? promise of specialness? sexual charge? sense of spiritual superiority? direct request for money, sex, loyalty, silence, or obedience? way in which my choices are being narrowed? way in which questioning is being equated with betrayal? way in which my resistance is being pathologized? way in which ordinary life is being downgraded?

old: Is the child part being seduced, scared, or rescued?
new: Who are you allowing to seduce, scare, or rescue your child?

old: Is the adult self still allowed to say no?
new: Are you allowing them to remove your ability to say NO?

old: Several yes answers mean slow down. Don’t deepen trance or make an irreversible decision. Return to the room, body, food, sleep, time, and counsel.
new: If yes to any of these, but especially if yes to more than one, you need to stop going deeper into trance or making decisions you can’t reverse, and come back into your room, your body, your food, your sleep, your time, and your counsel.

old: A good guide increases your adult self. A bad guide replaces it. A good guide can tolerate your no. A bad guide calls your no resistance, ego, fear, low vibration, trauma, sin, or proof that you need more of their guidance.
new: Good guides increase your adult self; bad guides replace it. Good guides are fine with you saying NO; bad guides frame your NO as resistance, your ego, fear, low vibration, trauma, sin, and evidence that you need more of their guidance.

old: Before accepting a recording or live suggestion, ask:
new: Before listening to a recording or before going into a live situation, make sure that the answer to each of the following questions is yes. If not, become fully alert, modify, or stop:

old: Was I plainly told that induction mechanics are being used?
new: Were induction mechanics plainly explained to me?

old: Can at least one answer lead to pause, modification, full alertness, or stopping?
new: Can my answers allow me to become fully alert, modify, or stop the process?

old: Does the speaker treat not noticing as secret proof that the process worked?
new: Is it hidden in a secret that not noticing is a proof of process?

old: Are roles, ownership, obedience, age, identity, or belonging being used to lower adult judgment?
new: Is a role or ownership, obedience, age, identity, or belonging being used to make me less responsible and to remove my adult judgment from the process?

old: Are fractionation, cues, later behavior, or memory effects disclosed before they are used?
new: Were fractionation, cues, later behavior, and memory effects plainly explained to me before the process?

old: Are ordinary body sensations being turned into evidence for a hidden claim?
new: Were somatic argumentation mechanics plainly explained to me?

old: Does the exit restore ordinary identity, movement, orientation, and critical judgment—and plainly say that the session has ended?
new: Will the exit process restore me to my normal identity, movement, orientation, and critical judgment, and state plainly that the process is over?

old: When an answer is unclear, stay fully alert. Ask for the exact script, change the method, or leave.
new: If in doubt, become fully alert, ask to see the script, modify, or leave the process.

old: Anxiety is often a Protector trying to prevent danger, shame, abandonment, failure, exposure, illness, rejection, loss of control, or a feeling it believes would be unbearable. Don’t begin by cross-examining it. Help the body first.
new: Remember that the anxiety is coming from a part of yourself that is a Protector who believes they are trying to save yourself from something bad happening. Maybe they are trying to protect yourself from danger, shame, abandonment, failure, exposure, illness, rejection, losing control, or something that the protector believes will be unbearable for yourself. Rather than getting into a dialogue where it feels as though yourself is interrogating the protector, start with yourself by taking care of the body.

old: Body first. Inner child second. Inquiry third. Action fourth.
new: Always work with yourself by taking care of the body first, then the inner child, then doing some inner inquiry work, and then taking some kind of action.

old: Start with the hand-on-heart, hand-on-solar-plexus practice.
“Little one, you are not alone. You do not have to solve this. I am here now. The adult is listening.”
Don’t recite the words like an incantation you’re hoping the subconscious will grade. Say them the way you’d speak to a frightened child you actually love.
new: One of the things that can help is putting your hand over your heart and your other hand on your solar plexis and say lovingly, “You are a little one. You are not alone. You don’t have to fix this. I’m here now. Let the adult take this.”
Don’t say the words, just hoping that they will work on your subconscious mind. Say them to yourself like you are talking to a little child that you love.

old: Use this gently. Buteyko-style reduced breathing can help some people who overbreathe or panic, but don’t force breath holds. Air hunger can briefly increase anxiety before it settles, so go slowly.
new: NOTE: There are some good things to be said for slowing down the breathing, especially for overbreathers and those subject to panic. Some of this is based on the Buteyko approach. However, it should not be forced, and creating air hunger can increase anxiety for a short period. Take things slowly.

old: Breathe through the nose. Let the inhale be small. Let the exhale be quiet. Pause only if comfortable. Let the breath become less dramatic. Stop if dizzy, strained, panicky, or medically concerned.
new: Try breathing through the nose. Try small inhales. Try quiet exhales. Try pausing if it is comfortable. See if it is possible to quiet the breathing. STOP if this creates dizziness, strain, a sense of panic or any other medical concerns.

old: EFT can be a simple bodily ritual: name the fear, tap gently, and stay in contact with what you feel. The evidence is still developing. A 2025 systematic review found seven randomized controlled trials involving EFT for anxiety disorders; EFT beat no intervention in several of them, although the evidence should still be treated cautiously beside first-line therapies.
new: One of the simplest aspects of EFT is that it’s something you can do in your body. If you’re worried about something, you can name it, tap on your body, and get in touch with the feeling. There isn’t a ton of evidence, but a 2025 systematic review of EFT and anxiety disorders found seven randomized control trials and noted that EFT was more effective than no intervention in several studies. While it should be handled with a bit of caution, it’s something to keep in mind if you’re not responding to first-line therapies.

old: “Even though this anxiety is here, I am willing to be kind to the part of me that is afraid.”
new: Even though I have this anxiety, I am willing to be kind to myself.

old: “What is the felt sense of this whole anxiety?”
new: Do all of these with the felt sense of the whole:

old: Don’t answer from the head immediately. Give the body time to form one vague sense of the whole situation, then ask:
new: Give it time to get one vague sense of the whole. Then, ask:

old: “What would this felt sense like me to know?”
new: “What would this like me to know?” etc.

old: Try a word or phrase and check how well it fits the felt sense. Then examine what it suggests about the situation; feeling right doesn’t settle that. Words and bodily attention can help correct each other.
new: Try out a word or phrase to see if it fits, but also look at what it says about the situation. A word that feels ok might say something that doesn’t fit. It’s good to use both to correct each other.

old: Sometimes the mind is too activated to meditate usefully. Then help through the body: foot, scalp, temple, neck, or shoulder massage; warmth; pressure; a weighted blanket; darkness; familiar calming music; or a massage gun used carefully. Avoid the front of the neck, injuries, numb areas, bruises, inflamed tissue, recent surgery sites, varicose veins, and anything that produces pain, dizziness, tingling, or a symptom that feels wrong.
new: Sometimes the mind is too activated to let meditation to take care of it. It may be useful to start from the body instead. Consider massage, either self or given by someone else, as the first resort. Maybe massage the top of one foot with the other, or the scalp, or a temple, or the back of the neck, or the top of a shoulder, or whatever feels good to touch. (Avoid the front of the neck. Avoid injured, numb, bruised, inflamed, recently surgically-operated-on areas, and varicose veins. Stop if it makes the anxiety symptoms or anything else feel bad, whether immediately or later, such as painful, dizzy, tingly, etc.) Other body approaches that may help include heat, pressure, weighted blanket, darkness, favorite calming music, massage gun, etc.

old: Other people settle with warmth, darkness, music, massage, weighted blankets, breathwork, familiar objects, or personal relaxation technology. Use the support that actually helps rather than assembling a tiny wellness trade show around the anxiety.
new: Others mentioned warmth, darkness, favorite music, massage, weighted blanket, breathwork, favorite object, and favorite personal technology.

old: Personal relaxation-tech note: On my ZHoly3O page, I discuss ozonated charcoal “holy water” as one relaxation support, and I also mention Blushield. These remain optional supports. They don’t prove that any inner signal is true. Stabilize the body, listen gently, reality-test, and return to one grounded action.
new: Regarding personal technology, see the ZHoly3O page for information about holy water (ozonated charcoal), and also mention Blushield.

old: First, body. Feet, chair, breath, room.
new: I will re-inhabit my body: first my feet, and my chair, and my breath, and the room around me.

old: Little one, I am here. Protector, thank you for warning me. You do not have to scream for me to listen.
new: When this is done, if there is a little person, I will reassure him: "It's okay, you're safe now, I'm here. Thank you, protector, for alerting me; you don't have to scream, I can hear you."

old: If there is real action needed, show me one step. If there is no action needed, help the body stand down gently.
new: Then I will see if there is anything I need to do. If there is, I'll just pick the first little thing to do, and do that. If there's nothing I need to do, I'll see if I can help my body stand down.

old: I will not abandon the signal. I will not worship the signal. I will listen, test, and act.
new: Either way, I don't abandon the signal, or worship it -- I'll do something.

old: The personal accounts and the way I arrange this practice are mine. The revised teaching brings them together with body-oriented and hypnotic approaches described below. That combination is an adaptation, not a treatment validated as a whole. These notes are for readers who want to follow an idea further; you don’t need them open while practicing.
new: The views and opinions expressed here are solely those of the author. Be aware that this is a re-vised form of teaching the above mentioned practice. The following is a body orientated combined with the hypnotic approach as described below. This is merely how I have found it useful to adapt the practice. I do not claim that the process in its entirety has been validated. These notes are not required to be used during the practice.

old: Maggie Phillips and Claire Frederick, Healing the Divided Self (1995), especially pp.24–27, 45–50, and 83–90, discusses interactive hypnosis, sensory learning, self-hypnosis, and a definite return. It is a professional clinical book, not a self-help manual; its case procedures and historical claims shouldn’t be imported wholesale into solo practice. Adam Eason and Benjamin Parris’s ISH article on self-hypnosis discusses self-directed learning and its relationship to another hypnotist and recordings.
new: Maggie Phillips and Claire Frederick in Healing the Divided Self (1995), pp 24-27, 45-50, 83-90, deal with some aspects of interactive hypnosis such as helping the subject learn how to use other senses in the learning process, developing self-hypnosis and also a definite way of getting back into hypnosis when required. It is more of a clinical book for professional hypnotists rather than a self-help one, so be careful about trying to introduce the case procedures described to yourself. Also be careful about taking the historical information at face value. Adam Eason, with Benjamin Parris, has an excellent article on self-hypnosis in this issue of ISH, dealing with self-directed learning and the question of another hypnotist and recordings.

old: Phillips and Frederick, pp.53–57 and 96–100, explain pacing, utilization, metaphor, and associational cues. Nimja’s hypnotic-language tutorial and trigger tutorial describe language and cueing techniques. They are technique sources, not evidence that every NLP claim is established or every example suits trauma work. The original wording and deliberately chosen re-entry sequence here are adaptations; Nimja did not write or endorse this guide.
new: The section on pacing and utilization is based on pages 53 - 57 of Phillips and Frederick's book, and metaphor and associational cues is based on pages 96 - 100. The information on hypnotic language patterns and triggers is sourced from Nimja's tutorial on hypnotic language patterns , and his tutorial on triggers . Please note that while the information in this guide is based on that in these sources, it is not identical to it, and has been adapted for a slightly different purpose. This is not something that Nimja has written himself, and should not be considered to be his endorsement of this guide. It is important that the words used here be kept identical, and that the order in which they are presented ( the re-entry sequence ) be followed exactly.

old: Peter Levine, In an Unspoken Voice (2010), chapters 5 and 7; Levine and Maggie Phillips, Freedom from Pain (2012), chapters 3–4; and Levine, Healing Trauma, chapter 4, inform bodily tracking, resources, titration, pendulation, and attention across sensation, imagery, behavior, emotion, and meaning. The invitation to try a movement or image is not a claim that a particular physiological repair has occurred.
new: Note: Parts of this post draw heavily from several chapters in In an Unspoken Voice by Peter Levine, 2010, particularly chapters 5 and 7, but also from chapters 3 and 4 of Freedom from Pain by Levine and Maggie Phillips, 2012, and chapter 4 of Healing Trauma by Levine. They discuss key ideas of tracking, resources, titration, pendulation and the range of foci of attention, from sensation, imagery, behavior, emotion to meaning, in depth. Also, although movements and images are offered for trying out here, they are not offered with the presumption that this is what is “fixing” anything physiologically.

old: The companion Inner Child Self-Love Reparenting Guide gives the fuller treatment of borrowed adulthood, love without compulsory trust, practical and relational repair, spiritual struggle, differentiation, and mutual peer support. The corresponding practices here follow that account while retaining the self-hypnosis entry, responsive language, and complete return.
new: There is a lot more information on borrowed adulthood, how to love without trust, working on this both in practical and relationship terms, working on the spiritual aspects, working on differentiation, working on this together with another peer, etc. in the companion piece: Inner Child Self-Love Reparenting Guide

old: Healing the Divided Self, pp.148–153 and 171–174, discusses renurturing, somatic work, and developing nurturing capacities. Levine and Maggie Kline’s Trauma Through a Child’s Eyes, especially chapters 4–5 and 10, discusses attunement and individual responses in actual children and caregiving. Applying those ideas to an adult’s younger feeling-states is an adaptation. My three-adult arrangement and borrowed-adulthood sequence are not presented as those authors’ tested protocol.
new: The information here is based on Healing the Divided Self pages 148-153 and 171-174 for renurturing work, somatic work, how to get nurturing etc. For information on attunement and how each child is different and needs to be responded to differently, see Trauma Through a Child’s Eyes by Levine and Maggie Kline, particularly chapters 4, 5, 10 which talk about actual kids. This method is adapted from that book to working with adult feeling states. The idea of doing it with three adults and going into borrowed adulthood in a certain sequence is not something that they have tried.

old: Nedergaard and Lupyan’s Not Everybody Has an Inner Voice (2024) studied people reporting different amounts of inner speech, not self-hypnosis adaptations. The questions in Quick start are a practical self-check, not a validated screening instrument or a test of hypnotic ability.
new: It’s worth noting at this point that the study that Nedergaard and Lupyan reference in their Not Everybody Has an Inner Voice (2024) was not investigating different adaptations of self hypnosis, but rather it was investigating people who reported having different amounts of inner speech. Thus, the questions in Quick start are not intended to be any sort of validated screening or test for ability to do self hypnosis, but merely a practical way to see if the ideas in this book are something worth trying out for yourself.

old: Levine’s Trauma and Memory (2015), chapter 7, is useful on the difference between compelling experience and historical verification. The VA’s hypnosis overview includes cautions about strong reactions and false memories. ASCH’s explanation of certification distinguishes professional preparation from a guarantee of someone’s competence. The existing links in the evidence and specialist sections point to their particular claims rather than validating every use of hypnosis.
new: Here are some links that may be useful. Chapter 7 of Barbara Oleah Levine's "Trauma and Memory" (2015) has a helpful discussion of this topic. The US Veterans Administration website has a good overview of hypnosis that includes some cautions about strong reactions and the potential of false memory creation: Here is a website from the American Society of Clinical Hypnosis (ASCH) that explains what hypnosis certification means. It is important to note that this is not a certification of competence: The links that already exist in the "Evidence and Hypnosis Specialists" sections also have some good information.
